passage: The regional badminton final was at nine the next morning, against the boy from Kitami who had beaten Hiroshi twice. "Sleeping?? Big day!" He turned the phone face down. He lost the final 21-14, 21-11, legs heavy, reactions slow. In the changing room he said loudly, "I was up till two. I was so tired I could barely see the shuttle." Astrid sat down beside him. "You said the same thing last time. Were you scared of him?" Hiroshi zipped his bag very slowly and didn't answer.

Dear Ayesha,
So, the district tennis final. I lost. 6-2, 6-3. Before you say anything, I was SO tired. I was up till 2:30 playing that farming game on my laptop, the one where you build the village? I kept saying one more harvest. Honestly, with proper sleep I'd have beaten Shalini easily. Everyone saw how slow I was.
Although... I keep thinking about why I didn't just go to bed. Amma told me twice. I think part of me was scared that if I slept well and still lost to Shalini, it would mean she's simply better than me. This way I've got a reason. But I also know I threw away my one real chance at the final. 😔
Write back soon? Tell me I'm not an idiot.
Kavitha

Tushar, don't even start. I know. Out in the raid, twice. Coach said 'Omkar, sit,' at half-time.
But you saw me, right? I was dead. I slept at three. I was on that racing game till three because I couldn't sleep anyway, so what's the point lying there? Kolhapur's defenders, everyone was talking about them all week, that big guy who ankle-holds everybody... Anyway. If I'd slept properly I'd have been fine. It was just tiredness. It's not like they're better than me.
Why didn't I sleep? I told you. I couldn't.
Okay, fine. Every time I closed my eyes I saw him catching me in front of the whole district. The game made that go away.
And then he caught me anyway. Twice. With my eyes burning.
Ugh. Next time take my phone at ten, Tushar. I mean it.

passage:
I'm Afreen, Jagdish's cousin. I was staying with them the week of the inter-school chess final in Lucknow.
The night before, Jagdish said, 'Early night, obviously.' At midnight there was still a phone glow under the blanket. At two I heard the little battle sounds of that tower game. When I whispered 'Sleep!', Jagdish said, 'Can't. Might as well.'
At breakfast Jagdish's hands shook round the tea glass, dark rings under both eyes.
Jagdish lost in the second round to a boy from Kanpur, a blunder with the queen. On the ride home, the first thing Jagdish said to Phuphi was, 'I'd barely slept, that's all.'
Maybe that's true. But all week before, Jagdish kept asking me what happens if you're rated high and lose early. I don't know what was going on inside. I just know which question kept coming back.

qa.q: What did Jagdish say first to Phuphi on the ride home?
qa.a: 'I'd barely slept, that's all.'

qa.q: What might Jagdish's repeated question about losing early suggest about Jagdish's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Jagdish was afraid a high rating could be shown up by an early loss; the late-night game may have supplied an excuse in case that happened.

qa.q: What choice could help Jagdish before the next big match?
qa.a: Talking openly about the fear of losing early and agreeing to put the phone away at a set time, so the match tests Jagdish's chess and not tiredness.

qa.q: How does Afreen's view from the next bed differ from what Jagdish told Phuphi?
qa.a: Afreen saw the phone at midnight, heard the game at two and remembered the worried questions all week, so 'I'd barely slept' looks to Afreen like only part of the story.

grounding: A cousin watches a teenager game late before a chess final and then blame lack of sleep, noticing the fear of losing underneath.
